1.quote_or_event: “During his reign he taught, for the benefit of the people, the seventy-two sciences, of which writing is the first, arithmetic the most important, and the knowledge of omens the last”
1.explanation: The Kalpa Sutra names Rishabha, the first Tirthankara, 'First King, First Mendicant, First Jina, and First Tirthakara', and credits him with giving humanity its arts, beginning with writing itself.
1.tie_back: Jain readers have long taken the Kural's 'Adi Bhagavan' (the Primal Lord) as Rishabhanatha, and this passage gives that reading a striking fit: the first Jina is also the one who taught the first of all sciences, letters.
1.source: Kalpa Sutra, Life of Rishabha §§210–211 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
1._accuracy_note: Quote verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; the Rishabha identification of 'Adi Bhagavan' is a Jain interpretive tradition, not settled fact, and Jainism holds no creator who is the 'origin of the world', so the fit is to 'first teacher', not first cause.

2.quote_or_event: “Without (right) faith there is no (right) knowledge, without (right) knowledge there is no virtuous conduct, without virtues there is no deliverance, and without deliverance there is no perfection.”
2.explanation: In the Jain 'road to final deliverance', mere learning is not yet right knowledge; it becomes so only when grounded in right faith in the truths the Jinas taught.
2.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says learning that is not anchored in reverence for the perfectly-knowing one (for Jains, the omniscient Jina) fails to bear its true fruit.
2._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; strong thematic fit, though 'right faith' in Jainism is conviction in the tattvas taught by the Jinas rather than worship of a deity's feet.

3.quote_or_event: “Then the gods prepared nine golden thousand-petaled lotuses, and put them in front of the Master in turn. The Master put his feet on them, two by two, and the gods quickly moved the others forward.”
3.explanation: Jain hagiography holds that when an omniscient Tirthankara walks, the gods set golden lotuses beneath his feet so that he moves upon flowers, one of the marvels (atishayas) of a Jina.
3.tie_back: This is the image behind the old Jain reading of the Kural's 'malarmisai ekinan' (he who walked upon the flower) as a Jina, whose feet the devotee is urged to reach.
3.source: Hemacandra, Trishashtishalakapurushacharitra, Book I (Adishvaracharitra), ch. III, 'Description of a samavasarana' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, 1931)
3._accuracy_note: Quote verified verbatim on wisdomlib; the Kural phrase is also read by Saiva and Vaishnava commentators as a lotus-seated deity, so the Jain identification is one interpretive tradition among several.

4.quote_or_event: “But a man who is indifferent to 'colours,' is free from sorrows; though still in the Samsâra, he is not affected by that long succession of pains, just as the leaf of the Lotus (is not moistened) by water.”
4.explanation: Mahavira teaches that love (raga) and hatred (dvesha) toward sense-objects bind karma and breed misery, while the one free of both, the vitaraga, stays untouched by sorrow.
4.tie_back: The Kural's 'one without craving or aversion' is exactly the Jain vitaraga, and this verse makes the same promise that freedom from both ends suffering.
4._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the verse describes the dispassionate person directly rather than refuge in a dispassionate Lord, which Jainism frames as following the Jina's example rather than receiving his grace.

5.quote_or_event: “Just as fetter whether made of iron or gold binds a person similarly Karma whether auspicious (punya) or inauspicious (Papa) binds the soul.”
5.explanation: Kundakunda's famous image teaches that meritorious karma is still bondage: a golden chain binds as surely as an iron one, so liberation means freedom from both punya and papa.
5.tie_back: It matches the Kural's 'two deeds born of darkness' almost exactly, naming good and bad karma together as the twin fetters that the soul must shed.
5.source: Kundakunda, Samayasara 146, as given in Saman Suttam 201 (English edition, Jain World)
5._accuracy_note: Wording verified verbatim in the Saman Suttam English translation (verse 201); the Samayasara gatha number 146 follows the standard numbering and was not checked against a separate full Samayasara translation.

6.quote_or_event: “The five senses, anger, pride, delusion, and greed—difficult to conquer is one's self; but when that is conquered, everything is conquered.”
6.explanation: King Nami, renouncing his throne, tells Indra that the real victory is over the five senses and the passions; the very word Jina means 'conqueror' in this sense.
6.tie_back: The Kural praises the one who 'quenched the five senses', and Jainism names its perfected teachers Jinas precisely for this conquest, holding up their path as the one to stand firm in.
6._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (Jacobi notes the verse does not construe smoothly); near one-to-one on sense-mastery, though the Kural's promise of long life is not the Jain goal.

7.quote_or_event: “he perceives, he knows, but there is no analogy (whereby to know the nature of the liberated soul); its essence is without form; there is no condition of the unconditioned.”
7.explanation: The Acaranga describes the liberated soul (siddha) as beyond every shape, colour, and sense-quality, so that nothing in the world can serve as its likeness.
7.tie_back: The Kural's 'one beyond all comparison' finds a direct Jain counterpart in the siddha 'without analogy', whom the Jain aspirant takes as the model that dissolves worldly anxiety.
7.source: Acaranga Sutra I.5.6.4 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884)
7._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the 'beyond comparison' match is strong, but the passage does not itself speak of relieving mental anxiety through refuge.

8.quote_or_event: “The body is the boat, life is the sailor, and the Circle of Births is the ocean which is crossed by the great sages.”
8.explanation: In the dialogue of Kesi and Gautama, the followers of Parshva and Mahavira agree that samsara is an ocean to be crossed by the boat of a disciplined life, which is why the Jinas are called Tirthankaras, 'ford-makers'.
8.tie_back: The Kural's 'ocean of virtue' that lets one swim the 'ocean of births' matches the Tirthankara, maker of the ford across samsara, whose path alone carries the soul over.
8._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim; the ocean-of-births image is shared closely, and the title Tirthankara itself encodes the crossing.

9.quote_or_event: “The Siddhas (or liberated Jivas) are void of karmas, possessed of eight qualities, slightly less than the final body, eternal, possessed of Utpada (rise) and Vyaya (fall), and existent at the summit of Loka.”
9.explanation: For the Digambara teacher Nemicandra, the liberated soul is defined by its eight qualities, its own nature uncovered once the eight kinds of karma that hid it are destroyed, not gifts from a creator. The same text opens by saluting the Jina 'with my head'.
9.tie_back: Jain readers take the Kural's 'en-gunattan', the one of eight qualities, to be this eight-fold perfected soul, so a head that will not bow before such a being fails at its highest use, like a sense that does not work.
9.source: Nemicandra, Dravyasaṃgraha, verse 14 (tr. Sarat Chandra Ghoshal, Sacred Books of the Jainas vol. 1, 1917; text at jainworld.com)
9._accuracy_note: Verse 14 checked word for word against Ghoshal's translation on jainworld.com. It fixes the Jain doctrine of the Siddha's eight qualities, but reading the Kural's 'en-gunattan' as a Siddha is a Jain interpretive tradition that competes with Parimelazhagar's Saiva list of eight attributes, and I found no scholarly source for that reading itself.

10.quote_or_event: “You have crossed the great ocean; why do you halt so near the shore? make haste to get on the other side”
10.explanation: Mahavira urges his chief disciple Gautama, who has come almost all the way to liberation, not to stall at the brink of the ocean of samsara but to finish the crossing.
10.tie_back: It shares the Kural's picture of rebirth as a vast sea that must be swum across to the far shore, reached by following the Jina's path to its end.
10._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim (the verse's refrain 'Gautama, &c.' is omitted); strong fit on crossing the sea of births, though Jainism stresses one's own effort on the path rather than reaching a divine Lord's feet.
